title: Anhydrous 0.1% retinal + 10% azelaic acid concentrate for blemish-prone skin: an 8-week split-face study
headline: A vehicle-controlled split-face study (23 completers, Fitzpatrick I-IV, company-authored) found small improvements in texture, redness and pores with a retinal plus azelaic acid combination; for anyone who already uses a retinoid and an azelaic acid, it adds nothing new.
evidenceTier: Small split-face RCT (8 weeks, vehicle-controlled); abstract read; full text not opened (no open full text)
fit: Weak. It combines two actives that a retinoid-using, pigment-conscious routine usually already covers separately, tested in lighter skin types and in a mostly young group.
displaces: Nothing is worth displacing: it would duplicate a retinoid step and an azelaic step.
estimateNote: Prices marked EST are my guesses, not looked up.
summaryPoints: Abstract (read): 23 participants aged 16-49 (mean 28), Fitzpatrick I-IV; active concentrate on one side, vehicle on the other, mixed with a moisturizer, 8 weeks. Texture improved 5.6% versus vehicle (p=0.0016); redness reduced 18.1% versus vehicle (p=0.011); pore parameter 22.3% better versus vehicle (p=0.015). Adverse events few and mild.
Measured with Antera 3D imaging and questionnaires; the improvements are modest percentages on an imaging scale and are not translated into clinician-graded acne counts.
All authors are affiliated with Skinome Research AB, a company; the product's commercial name was not given in the abstract and I did not identify a retail product.
Fitzpatrick V-VI and pigment outcomes (post-inflammatory marks) were not reported.
toneData: Fitzpatrick I-IV only; V-VI not included
fitLine: Duplicates existing retinoid and azelaic acid steps; light-skin trial; company-authored.
timeline: 8-week study; participants reported visible change within 4 weeks (65%)

fitAxes.why: Not measured; retinal plus azelaic acid is an irritation risk in principle (my inference).
It is itself a retinoid; stacking it on another retinoid is the wrong direction.
The study population was blemish-prone; acne counts were not the main outcome.
